newsitem.title: USA: Texas meet to focus on fast-growing LPG market.
newsitem.headline: Texas meet to focus on fast-growing LPG market.

text.p: U.S. and international players in the liquified petroleum gas (LPG) market open a two-day annual conference here on Wednesday to focus on the fast-paced growth of this market that drives the petrochemical industry.

The seminar, sponsored by oil consultants Purvin & Gertz, comes after a year of extreme price volatility due in part to a strong rate of growth that for the tenth consecutive year outpaced petroleum products.

"The market is growing much faster than petroleum products and the focus of this year's conference is to review the factors that have affected the market and how they will affect it in the future," said Rick Haun, a Purvin & Gertz vice president and director.

The liquefied petroleum gas market has grown an average of about 3.8 percent per year for the past ten years, compared to 1.6 pct growth in oil products. The materials are used by petrochemical companies to make a wide range of plastics from containors to dashboards, and other products, such as anti-freeze.
But some traders and analysts say that with the continued rate of growth, the LPG market has increasingly run up against constraints such as a lack of storage space.

"There is a much higher likelihood of price spikes because supply and demand has increased but storage has not. There is less of a margin of error in the supply system now than five years ago," said Houston-based analyst Dan Lippe, of Petral Consulting Co.
Few would disagree that one of the biggest impacts on the market this year was the crippling explosion at Mexico's largest gas processing plant at Cactus in July of last year.
The explosion sent U.S. prices up by more than three percent and kept a floor under values as Mexico moved to fill the gap left by the idled plant.
In addition, concerns about low inventories going into the winter heating season -- when demand traditionally peaks -- and the higher price of crude also kept the market bullish, traders said.
Average prices of propane, somewhat of an LPG benchmark, ballooned about 30 percent last year, from 32.10 cents in 1995 to 42.16 cents in 1996.

"The market has been very tough to gauge this year," said one Houston player attending the conference. "There were a lot of bullish pressures. Inventories were a concern and Mexico added a joker to the whole deal."

The conference opens with a worldwide LPG overview by Purvin & Gertz speakers and is to be followed by supply and demand outlooks from several companies including Dow Chemical, Shell Peru and Qatar General Petroleum Corp.
